Foundations: How You Communicate Today

You will see how a message travels from your mind to another person, where it gets lost, and how to choose the right channel. You will learn to recognise the four communication styles in real talk and in WhatsApp messages, and you will map your own strengths, hard situations and safety limits.
How a message travels: sender, channel, noise and feedback
Name the six parts of a simple communication model
Find the point where a misunderstanding started
Choose between face to face, phone call, voice note and text for a message

Many arguments at home, in the market and in meetings do not start with bad intentions. They start with a message that left one person's mind and arrived in a different shape in another person's mind. Communication scholars have drawn simple models of this journey since the middle of the last century. You do not need the theory, but one plain picture helps you find where things went wrong.
Two people talking with speech bubbles between them
Every conversation is a message sent, received and checked, again and again.

In the example, the buyer heard "you are cheating me", while you meant "transport costs went up for all of us". The message was vague ("more", but how much?), the channel was rushed, and her money worry was noise. Her angry reply is not the end of the story. It is **feedback**, and feedback is useful because it shows you exactly what arrived.
The communication loop
Sender has an idea
Puts it into words
Sends through a channel
Receiver interprets it
Receiver gives feedback
Noise can enter at every step, so the loop only closes when feedback confirms the meaning.
Two kinds of noise

**Outside noise** is physical: a generator, a weak network that cuts a call, a busy road. **Inside noise** lives in people: tiredness, hunger, fear, old quarrels, assumptions about age or status, or simply thinking about something else. Inside noise is often the bigger problem. A wife who asks her husband about school fees just as he walks in from a hard day meets a lot of inside noise, even in a quiet room.
Choosing the right channel

Every channel carries some parts of a message and drops others. Face to face carries words, tone, face and body. A phone call keeps words and tone but loses the face. A voice note keeps tone but removes the chance to respond at once. A text keeps only the words, so the reader adds her own tone, often a worse one than you intended.
Best for
Weak for
Face to face
Feelings, disagreements, apologies, important requests to elders
Long lists of details people must remember
Phone call

Numbers and addresses that need to be kept
Voice note

Anything the listener must find again later, or listen to in a noisy place
Text or WhatsApp message
Times, amounts, addresses, confirmations, records
Delicate feelings, anger, bad news
Data and cost

Voice notes and video calls use more data than short texts. If the other person has costly or limited data, a short clear text plus a phone call for the sensitive part can be kinder than a five-minute voice note.
Close the loop with a feedback check

The most useful habit in this lesson is the **feedback check**: after an important message, ask the other person to tell you what they understood, or tell them what you understood. Do it warmly so it does not sound like a test. "Just so I know I explained it well, what will you tell the others?" puts the responsibility on you, not on them.
Worked example: fixing a cooperative meeting time
For example, Ngozi is secretary of a women's savings group of 20 members in Enugu. She sends a WhatsApp message: "Meeting moved to Saturday." Six members come on the wrong day.
She finds the noise: two Saturdays were possible, and three members read the message late at night and only saw the preview.
She rewrites the message with all the facts: "Our meeting is now Saturday 14th, 4pm, at Mama Chidi's shop. Not this coming Saturday. Please reply OK when you see this."
She asks for feedback: replies of "OK" let her count who has seen it. After a day, 17 of 20 have replied.
She calls the 3 who have not replied, because a call reaches people the group chat does not.
All 20 members know the correct date. The fix was not more words, but specific words plus a feedback check: date, time, place, a clear contrast with the wrong date, and a way to confirm.

When a conversation goes wrong, try walking backwards through the loop before you blame anyone. Was the message clear? Was the channel right? What noise was there? What did the feedback tell you? This calm review is the foundation for everything else in this course.

Everyone uses all four styles at different times. A woman can be passive with her mother-in-law, aggressive with her children after a long day, and assertive with customers. The goal of this lesson is not to label people. It is to notice which style you are using in the moment, so you can choose.

Assertive communication aims for an outcome both people can accept.

Openness plus respect gives assertive; openness without respect gives aggressive; hiding your needs gives passive or passive-aggressive.

A simpler way to remember it: assertive communication is **honest and respectful at the same time**. Passive is respectful but not honest. Aggressive is honest but not respectful. Passive-aggressive is neither: the anger is real, but it leaks out sideways.
Spotting the styles in WhatsApp messages
Text removes tone, so styles show up in word choice, punctuation and timing. Read these replies to a friend who asks to borrow your gele for a wedding and has not returned the last one.
Passive: "Ok no wahala 😊" (while you are upset inside).
Aggressive: "YOU ARE NOT SERIOUS. Return my things first before you open your mouth."
Passive-aggressive: "Hmm. Some people sha." or a seen message with no reply for three days.
Assertive: "I'm happy to help, but I need the blue one back first. Can you bring it on Sunday? Then you can take this one."

Notice that the assertive reply is not cold. It keeps the friendship, states the condition and asks a clear question with a time. Capital letters, many exclamation marks and voice notes recorded while angry usually push a message towards aggressive, even when you did not intend it.
Worked example: rewriting a reply to a committee chair

For example, Halima, a trader in Kano, is asked by her church women's committee chair to cook for 80 people at a programme in two days, on top of her shop work. Her first instinct is "Yes ma, no problem" (passive), then to complain to others later (passive-aggressive).
She names the facts: she can cook for about 30 people alone; 80 needs at least three helpers and money for ingredients.
She names her need: she wants to support the programme without losing two days of sales.

She drafts an assertive reply: "Ma, thank you for trusting me with this. I can lead the cooking if two or three women join me and the committee buys the ingredients. Alone, I can manage rice and stew for 30. Which would you prefer?"
She checks it against the four styles: honest about her limit, respectful in tone, gives two clear options, asks a question.
The chair assigns three helpers and releases money for ingredients. Halima keeps her shop open the day before and still serves the programme, and nobody is left guessing what she thought.
Assertive is not the same as loud

In many Nigerian homes and communities, softness, greetings and respect words like "ma" and "sir" are part of good manners. You can keep all of them. Assertiveness lives in what you ask for clearly, not in volume or rudeness. A quiet voice with a clear request is assertive.
Why we slide out of assertiveness

People become passive when they fear conflict, rejection or losing a relationship, or when they were raised to believe that a good woman does not ask. People become aggressive when they are exhausted, feel ignored for too long, or have seen shouting work. Passive-aggressive behaviour often grows where open disagreement feels forbidden. Knowing your own trigger helps: many people notice they slide to aggressive when hungry or tired, and to passive with anyone older or more senior.
To move back to assertive in the moment, pause and breathe out slowly before you answer.
Ask yourself two questions: what do I actually need here, and what does the other person need?
Say your need in one sentence, then ask one clear question.
If you are too angry to be respectful, say "Let me answer you later today" and set a time.
In the next lesson you will look honestly at your own patterns, and at the times when speaking up needs extra care.

Is now the right time to speak?
Am I safe here?
Am I calm enough?
Is the other person ready?
Speak now or plan a time
If the answer to the first question is no, your plan is safety first, not a conversation.
Good time, wait and prepare, or not safe
**Good time:** you are calm, the other person is not rushed or angry, you have privacy if it is personal, and you know your main point.

**Wait and prepare:** you are very angry, the person is drunk, hungry or in front of an audience, or you have not yet worked out what you want. Waiting is not passive if you set a time: "Let us talk about this tomorrow evening."

**Not safe:** the person has hit, threatened, controlled or frightened you before, or you fear they will. In this case, assertiveness scripts are not the right tool and the problem is not your communication.
When speaking up could put you in danger

If someone hurts you, threatens you, controls your money or movement, or makes you afraid, your safety comes first. Do not confront them alone to practise this course. Talk privately to someone you trust, a health worker, a religious leader you trust, a recognised women's support organisation or the police. Keep important phone numbers and documents somewhere safe. You deserve help, and getting help is a strong act of self-expression.
Your rights in a conversation

Assertiveness trainers often list basic rights that help people speak up. You have the right to say no without a long excuse, to change your mind, to say "I don't know" or "I don't understand", to ask for what you want, and to make mistakes and correct them. The other person has exactly the same rights. Remembering this keeps your assertiveness fair: you ask clearly, and you accept that the answer may still be no.
Cultural context is not an excuse to stay silent

Respect for elders, husbands, leaders and in-laws is valued in most Nigerian families and communities, and this course respects that. But respect describes how you speak, not whether you speak. You can kneel or bow, greet properly, use "ma" or "sir", choose a private moment and still say clearly what you need. Many communities also have respected go-betweens, such as an aunt or an elder, who can help carry a difficult message. Using them wisely is a skill, not a weakness.

Guided Practice: Listening, Expressing and Saying No

Now you practise the three core moves of self-expression. You will listen so people feel truly heard, express a feeling and a need without blame using the four steps of Nonviolent Communication, and say no to requests while protecting the relationship.
Active listening: paraphrase, clarify and summarise
Show attention with your body, voice and short encouragers
Paraphrase what someone said so they can confirm or correct it
Ask open questions that help the speaker explain more
Avoid the five common listening blockers

Self-expression is only half of communication. People are far more willing to hear your view after they feel you have heard theirs. **Active listening** means listening to understand the other person's meaning and feelings, and showing them that you understood. It is active because you do something: you attend, reflect, ask and summarise, instead of waiting quietly for your turn to speak.
A woman listening attentively
Active listening means showing the speaker that her meaning arrived.
The four moves of active listening
Active listening in four moves
Attend fully
Paraphrase the meaning
Ask open questions
Summarise and check
Each move gives the speaker a chance to confirm or correct what you understood.

**Attend.** Put the phone face down, turn towards the person, and use small encouragers: a nod, "mm", "I see", "go on". In many cultures steady eye contact with an elder can feel disrespectful, so soft, occasional eye contact with a respectful posture is fine.
**Paraphrase.** Say back the main point in your own words: "So the supplier delivered late twice, and now you are worried about your Christmas orders." You are not agreeing yet; you are checking.

**Ask open questions.** Open questions start with what, how, which or tell me, and invite a full answer: "What worries you most about it?" Closed questions get yes or no and are useful only for checking facts: "Was it on Tuesday?"

**Summarise.** At the end, pull the main points together and check: "Let me be sure I have it: three things, the late delivery, the cost, and that you don't want to lose this customer. Did I miss anything?"
Reflecting feelings, not only facts

Good listeners also notice the feeling under the words and name it gently, as a question: "You sound really tired of this. Is that right?" If you guess wrong, the speaker will correct you, and that is fine; the correction still helps her feel understood. Avoid telling people what they feel as if you know: "You are just jealous" is a judgement, not a reflection.

Worked example: a teenage daughter and a school problem
For example, Grace, a mother in Port Harcourt, notices her 15-year-old daughter Ebi is quiet after school. Her old habit was to ask "What is wrong with you?" and then lecture.
Attend: Grace waits until dinner is finished, sits beside Ebi and says, "You've been quiet today. I'm here if you want to talk."
Ebi says some girls laughed at her answer in class. Grace paraphrases: "So you answered a question and some girls laughed at you."
She reflects the feeling as a question: "That sounds embarrassing. Is that how it felt?" Ebi nods and adds that it happens often.
She asks an open question instead of fixing: "What would help you most right now?"
She summarises: "So it happens often, it makes you not want to answer in class, and you want me to know but not to go to the school yet. Have I got it?"
Ebi talks for ten minutes, which is longer than usual. Grace learns it is a repeated pattern, and they agree to talk again on Friday and decide together whether to speak to the class teacher.
Listening when you disagree

Active listening is hardest when you strongly disagree, and that is exactly when it is most useful. Understanding is not the same as agreeing. You can say, "So your view is that the levy should rise to ₦2,000 because the hall rent went up. I see it differently, but let me first check I have your reasons right." The other person relaxes because she feels heard, and she is then far more likely to listen to your reasons in return. A simple rule many groups use: before you reply, summarise the last speaker's point to her satisfaction.
Listening on WhatsApp

Active listening works in text too. Before replying to a long or emotional message, quote the key line and paraphrase it: "You said the payment hasn't come since March. Is that right?" This prevents arguing about the wrong problem.

Saying what you feel and need: the four steps of Nonviolent Communication
Separate an observation from a judgement
Name a real feeling instead of an accusation disguised as a feeling
Connect your feeling to a need
Make a clear, doable request rather than a demand

Many of us were taught to hide feelings or to express them as blame: "You don't respect me", "You people never care". Blame makes the listener defend herself, so your real need gets lost. The psychologist Marshall Rosenberg developed a method called **Nonviolent Communication (NVC)**, described in his book *Nonviolent Communication: A Language of Life*. Its four steps help you say difficult things in a way people can actually hear.
A speaking head
NVC gives your words a clear order: what happened, how you feel, what you need, what you ask.
The four NVC steps
Observation: what happened
Feeling: how I feel
Need: what matters to me
Request: what I ask
Say them in this order, in your own natural words.
Step 1: observation, not judgement

An observation is what a video camera would record. A judgement adds your interpretation. "You are lazy" is a judgement. "The plates from last night were still in the sink this morning" is an observation. Words like always, never, lazy, selfish and careless almost always signal judgement. Observations are harder to argue with, so the conversation moves forward.
Judgement
Observation
"You never help me in the shop"
"This month you came to the shop on two of the four Saturdays you promised"
"You disrespected me in the meeting"
"When I started to speak in the meeting, you said 'sit down, we have heard enough'"
"That customer is a cheat"
"She took the shoes on 2 March and has not paid the ₦9,500 balance she promised for 9 March"
Step 2: a real feeling

A feeling describes what is happening inside you: worried, hurt, tired, frustrated, embarrassed, disappointed, relieved, grateful. Be careful with words that sound like feelings but really accuse the other person, such as ignored, betrayed, used, cheated or disrespected. They describe what you think someone did to you. "I feel ignored" invites argument; "I feel lonely and hurt" invites care. A useful test: if the sentence still makes sense as "I feel that you...", it is probably a thought, not a feeling.
Step 3: the need underneath

Every feeling points to a need that matters to you: rest, respect, fairness, support, safety, reliability, recognition, honesty, money to meet obligations. Naming the need moves attention from the other person's fault to what you both can protect. "I feel worried because I need to pay the rent on Friday" is very different from "You are making me worried".
Step 4: a request, not a demand

A request is specific, positive and doable now: who will do what, by when. "Please be more responsible" is too vague. "Would you be willing to come to the shop by 9am this Saturday?" is clear. Rosenberg's test for a real request is how you respond to a no. If a no leads to punishment or blame, it was a demand. If you are willing to hear the no and keep talking, it is a request, and people are much more likely to say yes.
Worked example: a sister and a family contribution

For example, Amaka, a teacher in Onitsha, agreed with her three siblings that each would send ₦20,000 a month for their mother's upkeep. Her younger brother Obi has not sent his share for two months. Her first draft: "Obi you are so selfish. You leave everything to me as usual."
Observation: "Obi, for August and September, I didn't see your ₦20,000 for Mama in the family account."
Feeling: "I feel worried and a bit tired,"
Need: "because I want Mama to have what she needs, and I need us to share this fairly as we agreed."
Request: "Would you be willing to tell me by Sunday what you can send this month, even if it's less?"
She checks the numbers: two missed months is ₦40,000 owed, but she asks first about this month, so the conversation can start rather than stall.
Obi replies that he lost a contract in August and can send ₦10,000 now and the rest in November. Amaka learns the real reason, and the agreement is renewed instead of the siblings falling out.
Make it sound like you

NVC can sound stiff if you copy it word for word. Keep the four parts but use your normal words, language and greetings. In Pidgin, Yoruba, Igbo or Hausa the same structure works: what happened, how you feel, what you need, what you are asking.

NVC is also a listening tool. When someone attacks you with blame, you can silently translate their words into the four parts: what did they observe, what might they feel, what might they need? Then you can respond to the need instead of the attack: "It sounds like you are frustrated because you need the order on time. Is that it?"

A **boundary** is a limit you set about what you will and will not do, give or accept. Boundaries protect your time, money, body and peace so you can keep giving where it matters. Many women find no the hardest word in any language, because saying yes has been rewarded all their lives. Yet every yes you give unwillingly is a no to something else: your children, your rest, your savings or your business.
A person giving a clear answer
A clear, kind no is better than an unwilling yes that turns into resentment.
The Yes, No, Yes structure

The negotiation expert William Ury, in his book *The Power of a Positive No*, describes a respectful no in three parts. First, a **yes** to what matters to you (your reason or value). Second, a clear **no**. Third, a **yes?**: an offer or question that keeps the relationship open.
A positive no
Yes: my reason
No: clear refusal
Yes?: an alternative
The first yes explains, the no is short and clear, and the final yes keeps the door open.
Worked example: a loan request from a cousin
For example, Zainab runs a small provisions shop in Kaduna. Her cousin asks to borrow ₦150,000, about the value of most of her shop stock. He did not repay ₦30,000 he borrowed last year.
Yes (her reason): "I'm keeping all my money in the shop this year because I'm building stock for my children's school fees."
No (short and clear): "So I can't lend you the ₦150,000."
Yes? (an alternative she is truly willing to give): "What I can do is ask my supplier if he needs a sales boy, or help you write to the cooperative about their loan."
She does not mention the old ₦30,000 here, because her no does not depend on it. She can raise it separately, as its own conversation.
The cousin is disappointed but not insulted. Zainab's stock stays intact, and he accepts her offer to ask the supplier about work.
Staying firm under pressure

Often the first no is not accepted. The other person repeats the request, adds guilt or brings in others. Two techniques from the assertiveness book *When I Say No, I Feel Guilty* by Manuel J. Smith help you stay calm.

**Calm repetition** (Smith calls it the broken record): repeat your main sentence in the same calm tone, without new excuses. "I understand. I still can't lend the money." Each new excuse gives the other person something to argue with.

**Fogging:** agree with any part of the criticism that is true, without changing your decision. "You're right, I did help Ifeoma last year. I still can't do it this time." There is nothing left to fight about.
**Ask for time:** you do not have to answer on the spot. "Let me think about it and tell you tomorrow" protects you from saying yes under pressure.
Do not over-explain
Long explanations sound like an invitation to negotiate. One honest reason is enough. You do not owe anyone a list of your expenses or your bank balance to justify a no.
Saying no up the ladder

With a parent, in-law, pastor, imam, boss or community leader, keep the structure but add respect: greet properly, thank them for thinking of you, choose a private moment, and offer a real alternative. "Ma, thank you for asking me. This month I am already committed to my shop every evening, so I can't lead the visitation team. I can bring drinks for the team on Sunday, if that would help." You have still said no, clearly.
A respectful no
Boss asks for unpaid weekend work again
"I've worked the last two Saturdays. I can't this weekend. I can stay an hour late on Thursday to finish the report."
Friend wants you to hold goods you can't store
"I'd like to help, but my room is full and I can't keep your bags. Shall I ask the woman next door who has a store?"
Relative wants to stay with you for three months
"You are welcome for a week while you find a place. After that I can't host you, but I'll help you look."

Expect to feel some guilt after your first few noes, especially with family. Guilt after a fair no does not mean you did wrong; it is often just the discomfort of a new habit. Check your decision against your reason. If the reason is still true, the no stands. If you learn something new that changes the picture, you are free to change your mind, and saying so openly is also assertive.

Holding boundaries gets easier with practice. People who are used to your yes may be surprised at first. Keep your tone warm and your words few, and most relationships adjust. If someone responds to a respectful no with threats or harm, return to the safety guidance in Module 1.

Two women can say the same sentence, "I need payment by Friday", and get completely different results. One looks at the floor and lets her voice fade at the end. The truth about 7-38-55

You may have heard that only 7% of communication is words, 38% is tone and 55% is body language. This comes from small experiments by the psychologist Albert Mehrabian in the 1960s. The studies looked at how people judged feelings and attitudes from single words when the tone or face disagreed with the word. Mehrabian himself has said the figures do not apply to ordinary communication. The useful lesson is narrower and true: **when your words and your delivery disagree, people believe the delivery.** If you say "I'm not angry" through clenched teeth, nobody believes the words.

Face, posture and culture

Body language is partly cultural. In many Nigerian settings a younger person avoids long direct eye contact with an elder, kneels or bows when greeting, and keeps hands still. These are signs of respect, not weakness, and you can keep them. Assertiveness shows instead in a steady voice, finished sentences and a calm face. Signals that weaken you in almost any culture include nervous laughter after a serious sentence, covering your mouth while speaking, apologising before every request and letting your voice trail off.
Worked example: practising a payment request with a voice recorder
For example, Ruth, a caterer in Jos, needs to ask a client for the ₦45,000 balance on a birthday order. She records herself on her phone's voice recorder app.
Recording 1: "Sorry ehn, I just wanted to ask, maybe if it's possible, about the balance?" It lasts 9 seconds, her voice rises at the end and she laughs nervously.
She removes the filler words (sorry, just, maybe, if it's possible) and writes: "Good afternoon, Mrs Bello. I'm calling about the ₦45,000 balance for the birthday order. Can you pay it by Friday?"
Recording 2: she slows down and pauses after the amount. Her voice still rises on "Friday".
Recording 3: she stands up while speaking, smiles before starting and lets her voice go down on "Friday?" so it sounds like a clear request.
She plays recordings 1 and 3 back to back to hear the difference.
The final version takes about 7 seconds, has no apologies or filler words and sounds calm and sure. Ruth makes the call, and the client sends the balance two days later.

Before sending an important voice note, listen to it once yourself. If you hear anger, rushing or a long ramble, delete it and record again, or send a short text instead.
Filler words and hedges

Filler words such as "ehn", "like", "you know" and "just", and hedges such as "maybe", "I think perhaps" and "if it's not a problem", make a clear request sound unsure. You do not need to remove every one, because some softness is polite. Remove them from the one sentence that carries your main point. A quick test is to write that sentence down and cross out every word the listener does not need. What remains is usually stronger and kinder, because it is easier to understand.

Difficult conversations with honesty and respect
Prepare for a difficult conversation using the three layers: what happened, feelings and identity

A difficult conversation is any talk you dread: telling an in-law her comments hurt you, raising a money problem in a cooperative, or admitting you made a mistake. The book *Difficult Conversations* by Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen, from the Harvard Negotiation Project, points out that every hard conversation is really three conversations happening at once.
A family together
The hardest conversations are often with the people closest to us.
Three layers of a difficult conversation
Identity: what this says about me
Feelings: what each of us feels
What happened: facts and intentions
Most arguments stay on the bottom layer, while the real heat comes from the two layers above.

**What happened:** who said or did what, who is to blame. People argue here, but each person usually holds only part of the story. Replace "who is to blame" with "what did each of us contribute". Also separate intention from impact: she may not have intended to hurt you, and you were still hurt.
**Feelings:** the hurt, anger or fear underneath. Unspoken feelings leak out anyway, through tone and sarcasm, so it is usually better to name them simply, as you learned with NVC.

**Identity:** what this situation seems to say about you. "Am I a bad daughter-in-law if I complain?" "Am I a failure because the contribution is short?" Noticing this layer calms you, because you can remind yourself the conversation is about a situation, not your whole worth.
Opening without starting a fight

The first sentence often decides the next ten minutes. Begin from what the authors call the third story: a neutral description that an outsider watching would accept, followed by an invitation. Avoid starting with your conclusion about the other person.
Opening that starts a fight
Neutral opening
"Mama, you are always insulting my cooking in front of people."
"Mama, can I talk with you about something that happened on Sunday? I'd like us to understand each other better."
"Treasurer, some of us are suspecting you."
"I've noticed the account balance and our records don't match by ₦12,000. Can we go through it together to find the difference?"
"You have finally shown your true colour."
"I think we see what happened at the shop differently. I'd like to hear your side, then share mine."
Worked example: a mother-in-law and public comments

For example, Chioma lives near her husband's mother in Owerri. At a family gathering her mother-in-law said loudly that Chioma's soup "has no taste". It is the third time this year. Chioma prepares using the three layers.
What happened: she writes the facts (three public comments, the last on Sunday in front of guests) and admits her part: she has never said anything, so her mother-in-law may not know it hurts.
Feelings: embarrassed and hurt, and a little angry.
Identity: she notices she fears being seen as a disrespectful wife. She reminds herself that a respectful private talk is not disrespect.
She chooses a private moment on a weekday afternoon, greets properly and opens neutrally: "Mama, can I share something that has been on my mind since Sunday?"

She uses NVC: "When my soup was described as tasteless in front of the guests, I felt embarrassed. I want to learn your way of cooking. Would you be willing to tell me privately what to change, instead of in front of people?"
Her mother-in-law says she meant it as a joke, but agrees, and offers to show Chioma how she prepares ofe owerri. The relationship becomes warmer, not colder.
A sincere apology

Sometimes the difficult conversation is your apology. A sincere apology names what you did, takes responsibility without "but", acknowledges the effect, offers repair and commits to change. "I'm sorry I shared your news in the group before you were ready. That was your story to tell, and I embarrassed you. I've deleted the message, and I won't share your private matters again." Avoid "I'm sorry if you were offended", which quietly puts the problem back on the other person.
Ethical limits of self-expression

Speaking up is never a licence to gossip, shame people publicly, record or screenshot private conversations to use against someone, threaten, or twist facts to win. Keep other people's private information private, including health, money and family matters shared in confidence. Honest and respectful means both, always.

Timing matters as much as words. Avoid starting a hard talk when either person is hungry, rushed, in front of an audience or late at night. If emotions rise too high during the talk, it is fine to pause: "I want to get this right. Can we continue tomorrow after work?"

Not every difficult conversation ends in agreement. Success means you said what was true for you, listened to what was true for the other person, and left the relationship as healthy as possible. Sometimes the best result is "we see this differently, and we can still work together."

You cannot improve what you never check. This lesson gives you two tools for evidence: a clear way to give and receive feedback, and a simple journal that shows your progress over weeks. Both will feed directly into your final project.
People exchanging feedback
Feedback is information that helps both people improve.
Giving feedback with SBI

The Center for Creative Leadership teaches a feedback method called **Situation, Behaviour, Impact (SBI)**. You describe the situation (when and where), the specific behaviour you saw or heard, and its impact on you or the work. It keeps feedback factual and avoids personal attacks, and it works for praise as well as correction.
The SBI feedback model
Situation: when and where
Behaviour: what you saw
Impact: the effect
Add a question at the end to hear the other person's side.
Vague feedback
SBI feedback
"You are not serious with this job."
"At yesterday's delivery (S), the three cartons arrived at 2pm instead of 10am (B). The customer waited and nearly cancelled her order (I). What happened?"
"Well done."
"In Saturday's meeting (S), you summarised both sides before the vote (B). People calmed down and we finished early (I)."
Receiving feedback well
**Listen to the end** without defending yourself. Breathe.
**Thank the person** for telling you. It took courage, even if the delivery was poor.
**Clarify** with a question: "Can you give me an example?" (Manuel Smith called this negative inquiry; it turns vague criticism into useful detail.)
**Decide** later, calmly, what is true and useful, and what you will change. You do not have to accept all feedback, but you should consider it.

Some feedback will sting, especially if it is delivered badly. Separate the message from the messenger: even an unkind comment may contain one useful point. Ask yourself, "If a friend I trust said this calmly, would any part be true?" Keep that part and let the rest go. If several different people give you the same feedback, take it seriously; if only one person says it, treat it as one view to test.

Spend five minutes, once a week, recording real situations. Use the same columns each week so you can compare. Keep it in a notebook or a notes app on your phone.

Three simple measures
**Asking rate:** how often you spoke up when you had the chance. Count chances and attempts each week, then divide attempts by chances.
**Self-rating:** re-score your ten-situation profile from Module 1 every four weeks, on the same scale, and compare totals.
**Outcome notes:** what changed because you spoke differently, such as money collected, a task shared at home, or an argument that stayed calm.
Worked example: four weeks of tracking
For example, Funmi (the hairdresser from Module 1) chose "asking customers for money owed" as her focus. Each week she counts how many times she asked directly and how much owed money came in.
Week 1: asked 1 time out of 5 chances, collected ₦3,000.
Week 2: asked 3 times out of 5 chances, collected ₦7,500.
Week 3: asked 4 times out of 4 chances, collected ₦8,000.
Week 4: asked 5 times out of 6 chances, collected ₦6,500.
Totals: she asked 13 times out of 20 chances, which is 13 ÷ 20 = 65%. In Week 1 the rate was 1 ÷ 5 = 20%; in Week 4 it was 5 ÷ 6, about 83%. Total collected: 3,000 + 7,500 + 8,000 + 6,500 = ₦25,000.
Funmi has clear evidence: her asking rate rose from 20% to about 83%, and ₦25,000 of old balances came in. She also re-scores "asking for money owed" on her profile: from 2 to 4.
Measure what you control

You control whether you asked clearly; you do not control whether the other person says yes. Count your actions first, such as times you used a positive no or a paraphrase, then note outcomes separately.

Keep your journal private. It may contain other people's names and family matters, so do not post it in group chats. When you use entries as evidence for your certificate, use first names only or initials.

At the end of each month, read your journal from the start. Look for patterns: which people or situations still push you to passive or aggressive, and which skills now come easily. Ask one trusted person for SBI feedback on a real conversation. These notes become the evidence in your capstone.

For example, Blessing, a nurse in Abuja, does every school drop-off and pick-up for her two children, even on her early shifts. Her husband Tunde works from home three days a week. Her first draft, written while angry: "You just sit at home doing nothing while I suffer."

Self-expression includes presenting yourself: at a women's meeting, a job interview, a training, a new church or mosque, or to a possible customer. Many capable women undersell themselves with "I'm just a trader" or say too much without a clear point. A simple structure lets you speak about yourself with confidence and honesty.

Present, Past, Future
A 60-second introduction

Past: how I got here
Future: what I'm building
End the Future part with a link to the listener or the occasion.
**Present:** your name and what you do now, in plain words.
**Past:** one or two facts that explain your experience, such as years in business, training or a key result.
**Future:** what you are working towards, and if it fits, what you are looking for from this group or person.

Spoken at a calm pace, 60 seconds is usually around 120 to 150 words. Write it, read it aloud with a timer on your phone, and trim until it fits comfortably. Prepare a 20-second version as well, for quick introductions.

For example, Aisha sells fabrics in Kano and is asked to introduce herself at a women's business network. Her usual answer: "I'm Aisha, I'm just a small trader."

Why this matters
Most quarrels start with a lost message
See where a message gets lost
Choose the right channel

Many arguments at home, in the market and in meetings do not start with bad intentions. They start with a message that arrived in a different shape in another person's mind.
You will learn which channel suits which message.
You will learn to recognise four styles of communicating, in talk and in WhatsApp messages.
And you will map your own strengths, your hard situations, and when speaking up is not safe.
How a message travels
Sender: the person with the idea or need
Message: what you said, not what you meant
Channel: face to face, call, voice note, text
Noise: outside, like traffic; inside, like worry
Feedback: the reply shows what arrived
Picture a tomato seller telling a regular buyer that prices went up. She is the sender.
She shouts, the basket is now more. That is the message. But how much more? The message is what you said, not what you meant.
The channel was a quick shout across the stall, to a buyer rushing for a bus.
Noise can be outside, like traffic or a weak network. Or inside, like the buyer's worry about money. Inside noise is often the bigger problem.
The buyer frowns and says, you people just increase anyhow. That is feedback, and it is useful, because it shows exactly what arrived.
Choose your channel
Feelings face to face, facts in writing
Face to face or call
Feelings and disagreements
Apologies
Important requests to elders
Text or WhatsApp
Times, amounts, addresses
Confirmations and records
Not for anger or bad news
Face to face carries words, tone, face and body. Use it for feelings, disagreements, apologies and important requests to elders. A phone call keeps the tone but loses the face.
A text keeps only the words, so the reader adds her own tone, often a worse one than you meant. Use texts for times, amounts and addresses. And remember voice notes use more data than a short text.
Worked example
Fixing a savings group meeting time
Close the loop: ask what they understood.
Find the noise: which Saturday? read late?
Rewrite with date, time, place
Add: not this coming Saturday
Ask everyone to reply OK
Call the ones who did not reply
For example, Ngozi is secretary of a savings group of 20 women in Enugu. She sends, meeting moved to Saturday. Six members come on the wrong day.
She finds the noise. Two Saturdays were possible, and some members only saw the preview late at night.
She rewrites it: Saturday 14th, 4pm, at Mama Chidi's shop. Not this coming Saturday.
She asks everyone to reply OK when they see it. After a day, 17 of 20 have replied.
She calls the 3 who did not reply, because a call reaches people the group chat does not.
The fix was not more words. It was specific words plus a feedback check. Ask warmly: just so I know I explained it well, what will you tell the others?
Four styles
Honest and respectful at the same time
Respectful but not honest. 'Ok no wahala' while upset inside. Resentment builds.
Aggressive: honest, not respectful. Passive-aggressive: 'Hmm. Some people sha.'
Honest and respectful. 'I need the blue one back first. Can you bring it on Sunday?'
Your friend wants to borrow your gele, but has not returned the last one. A passive reply is, ok no wahala, while you are upset inside. It is respectful, but not honest.
An aggressive reply in capital letters is honest, but not respectful. A passive-aggressive reply hides the anger in a hint, like, hmm, some people sha, or leaving her on read.
An assertive reply is honest and respectful at the same time. I am happy to help, but I need the blue one back first. Can you bring it on Sunday?
You can keep your greetings and respect words like ma and sir. A quiet voice with a clear request is assertive.
Safety first
If someone frightens or harms you, seek help. Safety comes first.
Speak now, or set a time
Before a hard conversation, ask first: am I safe here?
Am I calm enough? If you are very angry, say, let us talk about this tomorrow evening. Waiting with a set time is preparation, not avoidance.
Is the other person ready, or are they rushed, drunk, or in front of an audience?
Then speak, or plan a time.
If someone has hit, threatened or controlled you, this course's scripts are not the right tool, and the problem is not your communication.
Talk privately to someone you trust, a health worker, a women's support organisation or the police. Getting help is a strong act of self-expression.
Key points
Remember
Feelings face to face; facts in writing
Assertive: honest and respectful together
Start with a frequent, medium-risk situation
To remember. A message is what you said, not what you meant. Match the channel to the message. Close the loop with a feedback check. Be honest and respectful together.
And when you rate yourself, choose a focus situation that happens often and carries medium risk, not the hardest relationship in your life.

Three core moves
Hear others, then be heard
Listen so people feel truly heard

People are far more willing to hear your view after they feel you have heard theirs. So first, you will listen actively.
Then you will express a feeling and a need without blame, using four steps.
And you will practise saying no while protecting the relationship. Every unwilling yes is a no to something else, like your rest or your savings.
Active listening
Four moves of a good listener
Understanding is not the same as agreeing.
Attend: phone down, turn towards her
Paraphrase the main point in your words
Ask open questions: what, how, tell me
Summarise and check: did I miss anything?
Step one. Attend. Put the phone face down, turn towards the person, and use small encouragers like, mm, I see, go on. Soft, occasional eye contact is fine with an elder.
Step two. Paraphrase. Say back the main point in your own words. So the supplier delivered late twice, and now you are worried. You are checking, not agreeing yet.
Step three. Ask open questions. What worries you most about it? Questions that get only yes or no are just for checking facts.
Step four. Summarise the main points and ask, did I miss anything?
The common mistakes are interrupting, fixing too fast, and turning to your own story. When you disagree, summarise her point before you reply.
NVC step 1 and 2
Observation, not judgement
'You are lazy'
'You never help me in the shop'
'I feel ignored'
What a camera sees
Last night's plates still in the sink
Came on two of four Saturdays
'I feel lonely and hurt'
The psychologist Marshall Rosenberg developed Nonviolent Communication, or NVC. It starts by removing blame.
A judgement adds your interpretation. You are lazy. You never help me. Words like always and never make people defend themselves.
An observation is what a video camera would record. The plates from last night were still in the sink this morning. It is hard to argue with.
And name a real feeling. I feel ignored accuses. I feel lonely and hurt invites care.
Worked example
A sister and a family contribution
A real request can accept a no.
Observation: no share for August, September
Feeling: worried and a bit tired
Need: Mama cared for; sharing fairly
Request: tell me by Sunday what you can send
For example, Amaka and her three siblings agreed to send 20,000 naira each month for their mother. Her brother Obi has missed two months. Her first draft was, Obi you are so selfish.
Instead she starts with the observation. Obi, for August and September, I didn't see your 20,000 naira for Mama in the family account.
Then a feeling. I feel worried and a bit tired,
then the need. Because I want Mama to have what she needs, and I need us to share this fairly as we agreed.
Then a specific request. Would you be willing to tell me by Sunday what you can send this month, even if it's less?
If a no leads to sulking or punishment, it was a demand. Obi explains he lost a contract and can send 10,000 naira now. Use your own words and language.
Yes, No, Yes?
'I'm keeping all my money in the shop this year for my children's school fees.'
'So I can't lend you the 150,000 naira.'
'What I can do is ask my supplier if he needs a sales boy.'
The negotiation expert William Ury describes a respectful no in three parts. For example, Zainab's cousin asks to borrow 150,000 naira.
First, a yes to what matters to her: her shop money for her children's school fees.
Second, a short, clear no. So I can't lend you the money.
Third, an offer she truly means. I can ask my supplier if he needs a sales boy. Her cousin is disappointed, but not insulted, and her stock stays safe.
Under pressure
Staying firm, staying kind
Calm repetition, without new excuses
Agree with any truth; keep your decision
Ask for time: I'll tell you tomorrow
One honest reason is enough
Threats or harm? Safety comes first
Often the first no is not accepted. Repeat your main sentence in the same calm tone. I understand. I still can't lend the money. Each new excuse gives the other person something to argue with.
Agree with any part that is true, without changing your decision. You're right, I helped Ifeoma last year. I still can't do it this time.
You do not have to answer on the spot. Let me think about it and tell you tomorrow.
Do not over-explain. You do not owe anyone a list of your expenses. With elders, greet properly and choose a private moment.
If someone answers a respectful no with threats or harm, return to the safety guidance in Module 1, and talk to someone you trust.
Key points
Remember
Paraphrase and summarise so she can correct you
Ignored or betrayed are accusations, not feelings
Yes to your reason, a clear no, then an offer
Some guilt after a fair no is normal
To remember. Listen, paraphrase and summarise. Say what happened, how you feel, what you need, and what you ask. Give a positive no.
Some guilt after your first few noes is normal. If your reason is still true, the no stands.

Make your delivery match your words
Pace: slow down for the key sentence
Pause two seconds after your main request
Let your voice go down at the end
Drop fillers: sorry, just, maybe
No nervous laugh after a serious sentence
When your words and your delivery disagree, people believe the delivery. Fast speech sounds nervous, so slow down for your most important sentence.
Pause for two seconds after your main request. It gives it weight.
A rising pitch turns a request into a question. Let your voice go down at the end.
Remove filler words and hedges from the sentence that carries your main point.
You can keep kneeling, bowing and respect words. They are signs of respect, not weakness.

Difficult conversations
Three conversations at once
Ask what each of us contributed, not who is to blame. Separate intention from impact.
Unspoken feelings leak out through tone and sarcasm. Name them simply.
'Am I a bad daughter-in-law if I complain?' It is about a situation, not your worth.
The book Difficult Conversations, from the Harvard Negotiation Project, says every hard talk is really three conversations.
The first is what happened. Each person holds only part of the story. She may not have meant to hurt you, and you were still hurt.
The second is feelings. If you do not name them, they leak out anyway, through tone and sarcasm.
The third is identity: what this seems to say about you. Noticing it calms you. The conversation is about a situation, not your whole worth.
Your first sentence
Open without starting a fight
Starts a fight
'Some of us are suspecting you'
'You are always insulting me'
'Records differ by 12,000 naira'
'Can we check it together?'
The first sentence often decides the next ten minutes. Avoid starting with your conclusion about the other person. Treasurer, some of us are suspecting you, starts a fight.
Instead, describe it the way an outsider would, then invite her in. The account balance and our records don't match by 12,000 naira. Can we go through it together?
And choose a private moment, not when either of you is hungry, rushed, or in front of people.
Honest and ethical
A sincere apology, and limits
Never gossip, shame, threaten, or screenshot to use against someone.
Name what you did
Take responsibility, with no 'but'
Acknowledge the effect on her
Repair, and commit to change
Sometimes the hard conversation is your apology. Name what you did. I'm sorry I shared your news in the group before you were ready.
Take responsibility without but. Avoid, I'm sorry if you were offended, which puts the problem back on her.
Acknowledge the effect. That was your story to tell, and I embarrassed you.
Repair and commit. I've deleted the message, and I won't share your private matters again.
Speaking up is never a licence to gossip, shame people publicly, threaten, or record private conversations to use against someone. Keep other people's health, money and family matters private.
Give with SBI, receive with grace
Behaviour: what you saw or heard
Impact: the effect, then ask a question
Receiving: listen, thank, clarify, decide
The Center for Creative Leadership teaches feedback called Situation, Behaviour, Impact. First the situation. At yesterday's delivery.
Then the behaviour. The three cartons arrived at 2pm instead of 10am.
Then the impact. The customer nearly cancelled her order. What happened? It works for praise too.
When you receive feedback, listen to the end, thank the person, and ask, can you give me an example? Then decide calmly what is true and useful.

A five-minute weekly journal turns practice into evidence. Funmi counts how often she asked when she had the chance, and how much owed money came in.
In week 1 she asked once out of 5 chances, and collected 3,000 naira. Her asking rate was 20%.
In weeks 2 and 3 she asked more, and collected 7,500 and then 8,000 naira.
In week 4 she asked 5 times out of 6, about 83%.
Over four weeks, 25,000 naira of old balances came in. Count your own actions first, because you control whether you asked. Keep your journal private.

The one-page plan
Plan your conversation on paper
Goal and main point: one sentence each
Their side: what they may feel and need
A neutral opening
Request in four NVC lines
If they say no: repeat line and alternative
Write your goal: what you want to be different after the talk. Then your main point, the one thing they should remember, in one sentence.
Write their side. What might they feel and need? What will they say?
Write a neutral opening, and choose a calm, private time and place.
Write your request as observation, feeling, need and request.
And prepare for a no, with your calm repeat sentence and an alternative. Choose a conversation that is safe for you to have.
Worked example
Sharing the school run
Rehearse with role reversal: hear your words from the other side.
First draft: 'You just sit at home doing nothing'
Main point: share the school run
Their side: he may feel judged
Request: you do the run on your 3 home days
Added line: 'I know your work is real'

For example, Blessing is a nurse in Abuja who does every school run, even on early shifts. Her husband Tunde works from home three days a week. Her angry first draft was, you just sit at home doing nothing while I suffer.
Her main point: I need us to share the school run so I can manage my early shifts.
His side: he may feel judged for working from home, and his calls start at 8am.
Her request: this week I was late for my 7am shift twice. I feel stressed and worried about my job. Would you be willing to do drop-off and pick-up on your three home days?
In rehearsal, her friend plays Tunde and swaps roles with her. Hearing your own words from the other side shows which lines sound like blame.
Her friend asks, so my job is not important? So Blessing adds, I know your work is real and your calls matter. Tunde agrees to five of the six trips.
What, so what, now what
What? So what?
What happened and was said
What it shows about my skills
Where my style changed
Now what?
What I will do next time
The next step with this person
During the talk, paraphrase before you answer, say your request once, then pause. Close by summarising who does what and by when.
Within 24 hours, reflect. What happened? Then, so what? What does it show about your skills, and where did you slide into passive or aggressive?
Then, now what? What will you do next time? If it went badly, an honest reflection is still excellent evidence. Learning is the goal, not a perfect result.
Telling your story
Present, past, future
'I'm Aisha Bello. I sell Ankara and lace fabrics from my stall in Kantin Kwari market.'
'I started eight years ago with one bale. About half my sales are regular customers.'
'This year I want to supply tailors in bulk. If you know one, let's talk after.'
For example, Aisha in Kano used to say, I'm just a small trader. Now she starts with the present: her name and what she does, in plain words. No apology first.
Then the past: one or two facts that explain her experience. She started eight years ago with one bale.
Then the future, with a link to the listeners. This year I want to supply tailors in bulk. Two tailors approached her after the meeting.
60 seconds is about 120 to 150 spoken words, so time yourself and trim.
Evidence, not adjectives
Show a skill with STAR
Situation: records were 12,000 naira short
Task: raise it without accusing anyone
Action: private talk, neutral opening
Result: found the gap, two people now sign
Saying I am a good communicator proves nothing. STAR gives proof. Situation: our cooperative's records were 12,000 naira short.
Task: raise it without accusing anyone.
Action: I asked the treasurer privately, used a neutral opening, and suggested we check the records together.
Result: we found two unrecorded withdrawals, corrected the book, and agreed two people sign every withdrawal. Your journal and capstone give you true STAR stories.
